entries.title: printf and format specifiers
entries.summary: Formatted output to stdout (fprintf: to a stream, snprintf: to a string).
entries.description: A format is text plus conversions of the form `%[flags][width][.precision][length]conversion`. Arguments must match the conversions in number and type.

details.name: %d %i
details.text: signed int (use `%ld` for long, `%lld` for long long)

details.name: %f
details.text: double in decimal notation (`%.2f` = two decimals)

details.name: flags
details.text: `-` left-justify, `+` always show sign, `0` pad with zeros, space = space for positive numbers

details.name: width / .precision
details.text: `%5d` = at least 5 characters wide; `%5.2f` = width 5, 2 decimals; `%.3s` = at most 3 characters of a string; `%*d` takes the width from an argument

mistakes: `%d` with a `size_t`, `long` or double argument (wrong size/type: undefined).
Passing user text as the format (`printf(s)`): use `printf("%s", s)`.

entries.title: scanf
entries.summary: Formatted input; every argument is an address.
entries.description: Returns the number of items successfully assigned, or `EOF` if the input ended before the first conversion: check it. Whitespace in the format (and before `%d`, `%f`, `%s`) skips any amount of whitespace; `%c` does not skip (write `" %c"` to skip). The same conversions as printf, with one difference: `%f` stores a `float`, `%lf` stores a `double`. `%s` stops at whitespace; always give a width (`%9s`) for a `char[10]`.
mistakes: Forgetting the `&`: `scanf("%d", n)` writes to a random address.

entries.title: fgets, puts, getchar
entries.summary: Read a whole line safely; print a string with a newline.
entries.description: `fgets` reads at most `size - 1` characters, stopping after a newline, and always terminates the buffer with `\0`. The newline, if read, stays in the buffer. It returns `buf`, or NULL at end of file or on error. A line longer than the buffer is delivered in several pieces: a piece that does not end in `\n` (and is not the last of the file) is the start of a longer line. `puts(s)` prints `s` plus a newline; `gets` is dangerous and was removed in C11.
mistakes: Counting a long line as several lines.
Forgetting that the newline is part of the data.

entries.title: fopen and fclose
entries.syntax:
FILE *fopen(const char *path, const char *mode);
int fclose(FILE *stream);
entries.description: `fopen` returns NULL on failure (and sets errno). `fclose` flushes the stream's buffer and closes it; without it the last data may never reach the file. Streams are buffered (except stderr), so output written with `fprintf` may appear later than output from `write`.

details.name: "w"
details.text: write; creates the file or empties it

details.name: "a"
details.text: append at the end; creates it if missing

details.name: "r+"
details.text: read and write; the file must exist; not truncated

details.name: "w+"
details.text: read and write; creates or empties

details.name: "a+"
details.text: read anywhere, write always at the end

mistakes: Using "w" when you meant to keep the old contents.

entries.title: Reading and writing streams
entries.description: Text: line, character or formatted access. Binary: `fread`/`fwrite` move blocks of bytes exactly as they are in memory and return the number of ITEMS transferred; a short count means end of file or an error (tell them apart with `feof(f)` and `ferror(f)`). `fgetc` returns an `int` so it can return `EOF` (-1) distinct from any byte.
mistakes: Storing `fgetc`'s result in a `char` (an `EOF` can be confused with a data byte).
Writing `fwrite(buf, 1, sizeof buf, out)` at the end of the file instead of the `n` bytes actually read.

entries.title: fseek, ftell, rewind, fdopen, fileno
entries.summary: Move the position in a stream; convert between descriptors and streams.
entries.description: `whence` is `SEEK_SET` (from the start), `SEEK_CUR` (from the current position) or `SEEK_END` (from the end). `ftell` returns the current position; `rewind` goes back to the start. `fdopen` wraps an existing descriptor in a stream; `fileno` returns the descriptor of a stream (useful with `dup2`).
